claim: Fast directional growth is a necessity for the young seedling after germination to quickly penetrate the soil to begin its autotrophic life.
source: Fast directional growth is a necessity for the young seedling; after germination, it needs to quickly penetrate the soil to begin its autotrophic life.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about seedling biology and growth requirements.

claim: In most dicot plants, rapid escape from soil is due to the anisotropic elongation of the hypocotyl.
source: In most dicot plants, this rapid escape is due to the anisotropic elongation of the hypocotyl, the columnar organ between the root and the shoot meristems.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about dicot plant development.

claim: Anisotropic growth is canonically attributed to cell wall anisotropy produced by oriented cellulose fibers.
source: Anisotropic growth is common in plant organs and is canonically attributed to cell wall anisotropy produced by oriented cellulose fibers.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the field, representing the canonical view.

claim: A mechanism based on asymmetric pectin-based cell wall elasticity has been proposed for anisotropic growth.
source: Recently, a mechanism based on asymmetric pectin-based cell wall elasticity has been proposed.
evidence: This references recent work in the field proposing an alternative mechanism.

claim: Basic anisotropic information is provided by cellulose orientation in the dark-grown Arabidopsis thaliana hypocotyl.
source: Here we present a harmonizing model for anisotropic growth control in the dark-grown Arabidopsis thaliana hypocotyl: basic anisotropic information is provided by cellulose orientation) and additive anisotropic information is provided by pectin-based elastic asymmetry in the epidermis.
evidence: This is the main model proposed by the authors based on their experimental and computational work.

claim: Additive anisotropic information is provided by pectin-based elastic asymmetry in the epidermis.
source: Here we present a harmonizing model for anisotropic growth control in the dark-grown Arabidopsis thaliana hypocotyl: basic anisotropic information is provided by cellulose orientation) and additive anisotropic information is provided by pectin-based elastic asymmetry in the epidermis.
evidence: This is the main model proposed by the authors based on their experimental and computational work.

claim: Hypocotyl elongation is anisotropic starting at germination.
source: We quantitatively show that hypocotyl elongation is anisotropic starting at germination.
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' quantitative measurements of cell dimensions over time.

claim: Pectin biochemical differences provide important growth regulation in the hypocotyl.
source: We present experimental evidence for pectin biochemical differences and wall mechanics providing important growth regulation in the hypocotyl.
evidence: This is supported by immunolocalization data showing differential pectin methylation patterns.

claim: Wall mechanics provide important growth regulation in the hypocotyl.
source: We present experimental evidence for pectin biochemical differences and wall mechanics providing important growth regulation in the hypocotyl.
evidence: This is supported by AFM-based nano-indentation measurements showing elastic asymmetry.

claim: In silico modelling experiments indicate an additive collaboration between pectin biochemistry and cellulose orientation in promoting anisotropic growth.
source: Lastly, our in silico modelling experiments indicate an additive collaboration between pectin biochemistry and cellulose orientation in promoting anisotropic growth.
evidence: This is based on finite element method simulations showing enhanced anisotropy when both factors are combined.

claim: A 'wave' of elongation runs acropetally from the base of the hypocotyl towards the cotyledons.
source: This presumption is based upon measurements of cell length over time which indicate that a 'wave' of elongation runs acropetally from the base of the organ towards the cotyledons (Gendreau et al., 1997).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature and confirmed by the authors' own observations.

claim: The cell wall must change to allow growth of cells and organs.
source: Plant cells are contained within a stiff cell wall thus the cell wall must change to allow growth of cells and, ultimately, organs (Braybrook and Jönsson, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with a supporting citation.

claim: Growth may be generated by a cell wall which yields to (or resists) forces in a spatially differential manner.
source: With respect to cellular anisotropy, growth may be generated by a cell wall which yields to (or resists) forces in a spatially differential manner (Baskin, 2005).
evidence: This is cited from previous literature as a theoretical framework.

claim: The cell wall is a complex material with a fibrillar cellulosic backbone within a pectin-rich matrix.
source: The cell wall is a complex material with a fibrillar cellulosic backbone within a pectin-rich matrix (Cosgrove, 2016).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about cell wall composition with a supporting citation.

claim: Circumferential wrapping of cellulose fibers restricts transverse growth in Nitella.
source: In the alga Nitella, cell wall structure has been proposed to regulate anisotropy through the coordinated orientation of cellulose fibers within the wall: circumferential wrapping of cellulose fibers restricts transverse growth and the passive (or active) separation of fibers allows axial growth leading to anisotropy (Green, 1960; Probine and Preston, 1962).
evidence: This is cited from classic studies on Nitella as a model for understanding anisotropic growth.

claim: Passive or active separation of cellulose fibers allows axial growth leading to anisotropy in Nitella.
source: In the alga Nitella, cell wall structure has been proposed to regulate anisotropy through the coordinated orientation of cellulose fibers within the wall: circumferential wrapping of cellulose fibers restricts transverse growth and the passive (or active) separation of fibers allows axial growth leading to anisotropy (Green, 1960; Probine and Preston, 1962).
evidence: This is cited from classic studies on Nitella as a model for understanding anisotropic growth.

claim: Cellulose fiber orientation has been correlated with material anisotropy in Nitella.
source: Consistent with this concept cellulose fiber orientation has been correlated with material anisotropy in Nitella (Probine and Preston, 1962) and in epidermal cells of onion and Kalanchoe leaves (Kerstens et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from previous experimental work demonstrating the correlation.

claim: Cellulose fiber orientation has been correlated with material anisotropy in epidermal cells of onion and Kalanchoe leaves.
source: Consistent with this concept cellulose fiber orientation has been correlated with material anisotropy in Nitella (Probine and Preston, 1962) and in epidermal cells of onion and Kalanchoe leaves (Kerstens et al., 2001).
evidence: This is cited from previous experimental work demonstrating the correlation.

claim: Cellulose orientation perpendicular to growth has been demonstrated in maize and Arabidopsis roots.
source: Indeed, this has been demonstrated in maize and Arabidopsis roots, the wheat leaf epidermis, rice coleoptiles, soybean hypocotyls and onion scales (Baskin et al., 1999; Paolillo, 1995, Paolillo, 2000; Verbelen and Kerstens, 2000; Pietra et al., 2013).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies across different plant species.

claim: There are many exceptions where net cellulose orientation in the outer wall of the epidermis of elongating cells was not perpendicular to the axis of growth.
source: However, there are many exceptions where the net cellulose orientation in the outer wall of the epidermis of elongating cells was not perpendicular to the axis of growth. These include rice and oat coleoptiles, Arabidopsis hypocotyls and roots, pea epicotyls and dandelion peduncles (Paolillo, 2000; Verbelen and Kerstens, 2000; Iwata and Hogetsu, 1989; Roelofsen, 1966).
evidence: This is cited from multiple previous studies showing exceptions to the canonical model.

claim: Cortical microtubule orientation may act as a proxy for newly-deposited cellulose orientation as in most cases they correlate strongly.
source: Cortical microtubule orientation may act as a proxy for newly-deposited cellulose orientation as in most cases they correlate strongly.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge with some noted exceptions.

claim: In Arabidopsis hypocotyls, microtubules, cellulose-synthase complex movement and cellulose microfibrils orientation are correlated in epidermal cells.
source: Although some exceptions exist in root cells (Himmelspach et al., 2003; Sugimoto, 2003), the correlation has been very well documented in the case of Arabidopsis hypocotyls where microtubules, cellulose-synthase complex movement and cellulose microfibrils orientation are correlated in epidermal cells (Paredez et al., 2006).
evidence: This is cited from previous work establishing the correlation in hypocotyls.

claim: Transversely aligned microtubule orientation was observed in Arabidopsis hypocotyls on the inward facing epidermal cell walls and those of inner cortical tissues.
source: Most recently, transversely aligned microtubule orientation was observed in Arabidopsis hypocotyls on the inward facing epidermal cell walls and those of inner cortical tissues, while the outer face of the epidermis presented as unaligned (Crowell et al., 2011; Peaucelle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from recent studies showing differential MT orientation in different cell wall faces.

claim: The outer face of the epidermis presented as unaligned in Arabidopsis hypocotyls.
source: Most recently, transversely aligned microtubule orientation was observed in Arabidopsis hypocotyls on the inward facing epidermal cell walls and those of inner cortical tissues, while the outer face of the epidermis presented as unaligned (Crowell et al., 2011; Peaucelle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from recent studies showing differential MT orientation in different cell wall faces.

claim: Cortex cells exhibiting transverse cellulose or microtubule orientation could provide anisotropy to the epidermis through their physical connection.
source: Cortex cells exhibiting transverse cellulose or microtubule orientation could provide anisotropy to the epidermis through their physical connection.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on the observed patterns and epidermal growth theory.

claim: In growing plant organs, internal tissues can provide the force for growth but the act of growth only occurs once the epidermis, holding the tension, releases.
source: This sharing of information is consistent with the epidermal growth theory (for examples and reviews see [Baskin and Jensen, 2013; Kutschera, 1992, Kutschera, 2008; Kutschera and Niklas, 2007]): in growing plant organs, internal tissues can provide the force for growth but the act of growth only occurs once the epidermis, holding the tension, releases (Baskin and Jensen, 2013).
evidence: This is cited from the epidermal growth theory literature.

claim: Transverse microtubule or cellulose orientation in inner tissues alone has not been experimentally perturbed.
source: To our knowledge, transverse microtubule or cellulose orientation in inner tissues alone has not been experimentally perturbed and so this hypothesis remains unconfirmed.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the experimental literature.

claim: Treatment with cellulose synthesis inhibitors reduces cell anisotropy in roots and hypocotyls.
source: Disruption of cellulose orientation has mixed effects on cell-shape anisotropy: treatment with cellulose synthesis inhibitors reduces cell anisotropy in roots and hypocotyls (Desprez et al., 2002; Heim et al., 1991) with a developmentally stage-specific magnitude (Refrégier et al., 2004)
evidence: This is cited from previous experimental work with cellulose synthesis inhibitors.

claim: The mutant botero/katanin has defects in microtubule orientation and shows reduced cell length but maintains some anisotropy.
source: the mutant botero/katanin has defects in microtubule orientation and shows reduced cell length but maintains some anisotropy (Bichet et al., 2001)
evidence: This is cited from previous genetic studies showing that anisotropy is not completely lost.

claim: Mutations in cellulose synthase complex subunits cause a decrease in cell and organ length, but some anisotropy is maintained.
source: mutations in cellulose synthase complex subunits cause a decrease in cell and organ length, but again some anisotropy is maintained (Refrégier et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2003; Fagard, 2000; Fujita et al., 2013)
evidence: This is cited from multiple genetic studies showing partial maintenance of anisotropy.

claim: In some mutants early growth is normal when compared to wild-type (prc1-1).
source: in some mutants early growth is normal when compared to wild-type (prc1-1 [Refrégier et al., 2004]).
evidence: This is cited from a specific mutant study showing temporal specificity of effects.

claim: There may be more to tissue anisotropy than cellulose orientation alone.
source: These subtleties strongly indicate that there may be more to tissue anisotropy than cellulose orientation alone (Baskin, 2005).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the mixed effects of cellulose disruption on anisotropy, with a supporting citation.

claim: The transition from slow to rapid growth has been hypothesized to involve changes in pectin chemistry.
source: The pectin matrix of the cell wall arises as a strong candidate for regulating anisotropic growth as the transition from slow to rapid growth has been hypothesized to involve changes in pectin chemistry (Pelletier et al., 2010).
evidence: This is cited from previous work hypothesizing a role for pectin in growth transitions.

claim: Differential pectin rigidity within individual epidermal cells might dictate the onset of anisotropy.
source: It has recently been proposed that differential pectin rigidity, within individual epidermal cells, might dictate the onset of anisotropy (in the absence of epidermal MT orientation) (Peaucelle et al., 2015).
evidence: This is cited from recent work proposing pectin-based control of anisotropy.

claim: All hypocotyl cells were geometrically anisotropic from the time of germination, irrespective of position along the hypocotyl.
source: Also, in our system all hypocotyl cells were geometrically anisotropic from the time of germination, irrespective of position along the hypocotyl (Figure 1C; shape anisotropy, ratio of cell length to width).
evidence: This is a key finding from the authors' measurements shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Cell length was always increasing at a higher rate than cell width.
source: Calculations of relative growth rates for each cell index, over 6H intervals, revealed that cell length was always increasing at a higher rate than cell width (Figure 1D and Supplemental file 1; RGR(L) vs RGR(W)).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of growth rates shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The RGR(L) of cells within the acropetal wave was relatively constant (8.95% ± 0.56 per hour).
source: The RGR(L) of cells within the acropetal wave was relatively constant (8.95% ± 0.56 per hour; Figure 1D, Supplementary file 1), indicating that there was a transition from slow to rapid elongation within the wave but that growth rate did not increase over time as the wave moved.
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' growth rate calculations.

claim: The RGR(W) was remarkably constant in time and space (2.6% ± 0.2 per hour).
source: In contrast, the RGR(W) was, after the initial suppression, remarkably constant in time and space (2.6% ± 0.2 per hour; Figure 1D, Supplemental file 1).
evidence: This is a quantitative finding from the authors' growth rate calculations.

claim: Cells are geometrically anisotropic at germination in dark-grown hypocotyls.
source: Our data paint an accurate picture of dark-grown hypocotyl growth: cells are geometrically anisotropic at germination, their growth is always anisotropic, and the acropetal wave is only evident in the elongation of cells but not their expansion in width.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the authors' growth measurements.

claim: Cell growth is always anisotropic in dark-grown hypocotyls.
source: Our data paint an accurate picture of dark-grown hypocotyl growth: cells are geometrically anisotropic at germination, their growth is always anisotropic, and the acropetal wave is only evident in the elongation of cells but not their expansion in width.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the authors' growth measurements.

claim: The acropetal wave is only evident in the elongation of cells but not their expansion in width.
source: Our data paint an accurate picture of dark-grown hypocotyl growth: cells are geometrically anisotropic at germination, their growth is always anisotropic, and the acropetal wave is only evident in the elongation of cells but not their expansion in width.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the authors' growth measurements.

claim: At germination, basal epidermal cells exhibited a wide range of MT angles on their outer epidermal face with a slight transverse tendency (~30% presenting transversely between 0 and 10°).
source: At germination, basal epidermal cells exhibited a wide range of MT angles on their outer epidermal face with a slight transverse tendency (~30% presenting transversely between 0 and 10°; Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule angles shown in Figure 2.

claim: By 24HPG, the average angle on the outer face was slightly axial with ~31% of MTs being oriented between 80–90°.
source: By 24HPG, the average angle on the outer face was slightly axial with ~31% of MTs being oriented between 80–90° (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule angles shown in Figure 2.

claim: At 24HPG, MTs at cortex cell faces appeared more transversely aligned and presented ~41% between 0 and 10°.
source: At 24HPG, we could not observe MT signal at the inner epidermal face, but could at the adjacent cortex cell faces (a phenomenon consistent across all three marker lines, at this early stage). MTs at cortex cell faces appeared more transversely aligned and presented ~41% between 0 and 10° (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule angles in cortex cells shown in Figure 2.

claim: MTs at the outer epidermal face were weakly transverse at the time of germination.
source: From these data we concluded that MTs at the outer epidermal face were weakly transverse at the time of germination and those in inner cortical tissues were more strongly transverse by 24HPG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule angle measurements.

claim: MTs in inner cortical tissues were more strongly transverse by 24HPG.
source: From these data we concluded that MTs at the outer epidermal face were weakly transverse at the time of germination and those in inner cortical tissues were more strongly transverse by 24HPG.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the microtubule angle measurements.

claim: By 65HPG, the outer epidermal face exhibited a MT angle trend towards axial alignment (~32% between 80–90°).
source: By 65HPG, when hypocotyl cells were rapidly elongating, the outer epidermal face exhibited a MT angle trend towards axial alignment (Figure 2A,B; ~32% between 80–90°).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule angles shown in Figure 2.

claim: The inner epidermal face of 65HPG cells exhibited a transverse angle distribution (~44% between 0 and 10°).
source: The inner epidermal face of 65HPG cells did show MT signal and exhibited an transverse angle distribution (Figure 2A,B; ~44% between 0 and 10°).
evidence: This is based on quantitative analysis of microtubule angles shown in Figure 2.

claim: During anisotropic growth from the time of germination, MT-based anisotropy information likely came from cortex cells or inner epidermal faces.
source: These data led us to conclude that during anisotropic growth from the time of germination, MT-based anisotropy information likely came from cortex cells or inner epidermal faces.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the differential MT orientation patterns observed in different cell layers.

claim: At 4HPG, slower-growing epidermal transverse walls were marked by 2F4 and LM19 indicating the presence of de-methylated HG and calcium cross-linked HG.
source: At 4HPG, slower-growing epidermal transverse walls were marked by 2F4 and LM19 indicating the presence of de-methylated HG and calcium cross-linked HG (Figure 3A, orange arrow heads; see inset for naming convention).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 4HPG, the faster growing axial walls were marked with LM20 indicating the presence of methylated pectin.
source: In epidermal cells, the faster growing axial walls were marked with LM20 indicating the presence of methylated pectin (Figure 3A, gold arrow heads).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 24HPG, the asymmetry in 2F4 and LM20 antibodies was maintained.
source: At 24HPG, the asymmetry in 2F4 and LM20 antibodies was maintained, but the LM19 antibody marked both axial and transverse walls (Figure 3A; immunolocalization controls can be found in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: At 24HPG, the LM19 antibody marked both axial and transverse walls.
source: At 24HPG, the asymmetry in 2F4 and LM20 antibodies was maintained, but the LM19 antibody marked both axial and transverse walls (Figure 3A; immunolocalization controls can be found in Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Slowly growing transverse walls had more de-methylated pectin which was calcium cross-linked.
source: We concluded that slowly growing transverse walls had more de-methylated pectin which was calcium cross-linked, while faster growing axial walls had more methylated pectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunolocalization patterns.

claim: Faster growing axial walls had more methylated pectin.
source: We concluded that slowly growing transverse walls had more de-methylated pectin which was calcium cross-linked, while faster growing axial walls had more methylated pectin.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the immunolocalization patterns.

claim: At 4HPG, axial walls were more elastic (lower indentation modulus) when compared with transverse walls (18.4 MPa ± 1.9 vs 24.8 MPa ± 2.0).
source: At 4HPG, axial walls were more elastic (lower indentation modulus (IM)) when compared with transverse walls (18.4 MPa ± 1.9 vs 24.8 MPa ± 2.0; Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AFM nano-indentation measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 24HPG, the difference in elasticity between axial and transverse walls was still observed in basal cells (12.7 MPa ±0.4 vs 20.0 MPa ±0.8).
source: This difference was still observed in basal cells at 24HPG coincident with an increase in overall elasticity when they were entering into the rapid growth phase (12.7 MPa ±0.4 vs 20.0 MPa ±0.8; Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AFM nano-indentation measurements shown in Figure 3B.

claim: At 24HPG, cell wall thickness was not significantly different between axial and transverse walls of basal hypocotyl cells.
source: At 24HPG, cell wall thickness was not significantly different between axial and transverse walls of basal hypocotyl cells, indicating that elasticity difference were underlain by biochemical and not geometrical differences (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cryo-SEM measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The elastic asymmetry increased to a ratio of 2 by 48HPG.
source: The elastic asymmetry increased to a ratio of 2 by 48HPG (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AFM measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: A cell-level asymmetry in wall elasticity was present from the time of germination.
source: From these data, it was apparent that a cell-level asymmetry in wall elasticity was present from the time of germination, coincident with growth anisotropy, and correlated with changes in pectin chemistry in dark-grown hypocotyl basal epidermal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM and immunolocalization data.

claim: Cell-level elastic asymmetry was coincident with growth anisotropy.
source: From these data, it was apparent that a cell-level asymmetry in wall elasticity was present from the time of germination, coincident with growth anisotropy, and correlated with changes in pectin chemistry in dark-grown hypocotyl basal epidermal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM and growth data.

claim: Cell-level elastic asymmetry correlated with changes in pectin chemistry in dark-grown hypocotyl basal epidermal cells.
source: From these data, it was apparent that a cell-level asymmetry in wall elasticity was present from the time of germination, coincident with growth anisotropy, and correlated with changes in pectin chemistry in dark-grown hypocotyl basal epidermal cells.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the AFM and immunolocalization data.

claim: When the axial and transverse anticlinal walls had the same elasticity and no material anisotropy was specified, the pressure forces caused the maximal strain to be transverse.
source: When the axial and transverse anticlinal walls had the same elasticity (no asymmetry) and when no material anisotropy was specified (cellulose orientation was not coordinated), the pressure forces caused the maximal strain (and stress) to be transverse (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A 100-fold elastic asymmetry was required to drive axial anisotropy in the absence of cellulose-based material anisotropy.
source: In order to drive axial anisotropy, in the absence of cellulose-based material anisotropy, a 100-fold elastic asymmetry had to be invoked (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: A 2-fold elastic asymmetry alone, as measured in experiments, would be insufficient to drive anisotropic growth.
source: These results led us to hypothesize that a 2-fold elastic asymmetry alone, as measured in our experiments (Figure 3), would be insufficient to drive anisotropic growth.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on the simulation results compared to experimental measurements.

claim: When material anisotropy favoring axial strain was specified at the inner epidermal wall, axial growth anisotropy was obtained.
source: When material anisotropy favoring axial strain was specified at the inner epidermal wall (as measured in [Crowell et al., 2011]), we obtained axial growth anisotropy (Figure 4B)
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Addition of a 2-fold elastic asymmetry enhanced the magnitude of growth anisotropy when combined with material anisotropy at the inner epidermal wall.
source: strikingly, addition of a 2-fold elastic asymmetry, consistent with our experiments (Figure 3), enhanced the magnitude of growth anisotropy (Figure 4B,C).
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4B,C.

claim: Simulating internal tissue anisotropy by specifying axial pressure in the inner-epidermal space recovered axial anisotropy.
source: Since it was also possible that internal tissue provided anisotropic information (i.e. the cortex, [Hejnowicz et al., 2000]), we simulated this situation by specifying axial pressure in the inner-epidermal space and also recovered axial anisotropy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Addition of 2-fold elastic asymmetry enhanced the magnitude of axial anisotropy when internal tissue provided anisotropic information.
source: The addition of 2-fold elastic asymmetry in the epidermis was again able to enhance the magnitude of axial anisotropy (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a result from the finite element method simulations shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: Epidermal elastic asymmetry alone was insufficient to drive axial growth anisotropy.
source: In conclusion, our finite element mechanical model led us to propose that while epidermal elastic asymmetry alone was insufficient to drive axial growth anisotropy, it was able to contribute by increasing the anisotropy achieved when anisotropic information was provided by inner tissues or the inner epidermal wall.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: Epidermal elastic asymmetry was able to contribute by increasing the anisotropy achieved when anisotropic information was provided by inner tissues or the inner epidermal wall.
source: In conclusion, our finite element mechanical model led us to propose that while epidermal elastic asymmetry alone was insufficient to drive axial growth anisotropy, it was able to contribute by increasing the anisotropy achieved when anisotropic information was provided by inner tissues or the inner epidermal wall.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the simulation results.

claim: PME5 induction increased the rigidity in both axial and transverse anticlinal walls.
source: We observed that both PME5 and PMEI3 induction abolished cell-level elastic asymmetry: PME5 increased the rigidity in both axial and transverse anticlinal walls, while PMEI3 decreased the rigidity in both (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AFM measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: PMEI3 induction decreased the rigidity in both axial and transverse anticlinal walls.
source: We observed that both PME5 and PMEI3 induction abolished cell-level elastic asymmetry: PME5 increased the rigidity in both axial and transverse anticlinal walls, while PMEI3 decreased the rigidity in both (Figure 5A; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on AFM measurements shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Induction of PMEI3 led to more anisotropic cells within the elongation wave.
source: These changes in cell wall elastic asymmetry were accompanied by changes in cell shape anisotropy: induction of PMEI3 led to more anisotropic cells within the elongation wave and PME5 induction to less anisotropic cells (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cell shape measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: PME5 induction led to less anisotropic cells.
source: These changes in cell wall elastic asymmetry were accompanied by changes in cell shape anisotropy: induction of PMEI3 led to more anisotropic cells within the elongation wave and PME5 induction to less anisotropic cells (Figure 5B; Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is based on cell shape measurements shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The position of the wave was not altered with PMEI3 induction.
source: Note that the position of the wave was not altered with PMEI3 induction, indicating that ectopically altering pectin chemistry could alter growth rate but not the position of the acropetal wave.
evidence: This is an observation from the cell shape data in Figure 5B.

claim: Anisotropy was not lost in either transgenic induction indicating that loss of cell wall asymmetry alone is not enough to abolish anisotropic cell shape.
source: Also, anisotropy was not lost in either transgenic induction indicating that loss of cell wall asymmetry alone is not enough to abolish anisotropic cell shape, or presumably growth.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the observation that cells remained anisotropic despite loss of elastic asymmetry.

claim: PME5 induction abolished the rapid elongation phase.
source: When NT, PME5 and PMEI3 hypocotyls were exposed to the inducer the following changes in growth were observed at the organ level: when compared to NT, PME5 induction abolished the rapid elongation phase and PMEI3 induction increased early elongation essentially flattening out the difference between the slow and rapid phases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on hypocotyl length measurements over time shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PMEI3 induction increased early elongation essentially flattening out the difference between the slow and rapid phases.
source: When NT, PME5 and PMEI3 hypocotyls were exposed to the inducer the following changes in growth were observed at the organ level: when compared to NT, PME5 induction abolished the rapid elongation phase and PMEI3 induction increased early elongation essentially flattening out the difference between the slow and rapid phases (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is based on hypocotyl length measurements over time shown in Figure 5C.

claim: PME5 induction resulted in a reduced hypocotyl length and a reduction in hypocotyl width.
source: Commensurate with the change in cell-level anisotropy, PME5 induction resulted in a reduced hypocotyl length (Figure 5C) and also a reduction in hypocotyl width (Figures 5D, 24 and 48HPG).
evidence: This is based on hypocotyl measurements shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: PMEI3 induction led to an increase in hypocotyl length and an increase in hypocotyl width.
source: Conversely, induction of PMEI3 led to an increase in hypocotyl length (Figure 5C) and an increase in hypocotyl width (Figures 5D, 24 and 48HPG).
evidence: This is based on hypocotyl measurements shown in Figures 5C and 5D.

claim: NT control hypocotyls treated with oryzalin showed a reduction in cell shape anisotropy indicating typical cell swelling.
source: NT control hypocotyls, treated with the inducer, showed a reduction in cell shape anisotropy when treated with oryzalin indicating typical cell swelling (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on cell shape measurements in oryzalin-treated hypocotyls shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The effect of oryzalin on cell swelling was reduced in induced PME5 plants.
source: This effect was reduced in induced PME5 plants and enhanced in induced PMEI3 plants (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on cell shape measurements in oryzalin-treated hypocotyls shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: The effect of oryzalin on cell swelling was enhanced in induced PMEI3 plants.
source: This effect was reduced in induced PME5 plants and enhanced in induced PMEI3 plants (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is based on cell shape measurements in oryzalin-treated hypocotyls shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: Changes in pectin biochemistry could modulate the effect of MT-derived cell swelling and isotropy.
source: These data indicated that changes in pectin biochemistry could modulate the effect of MT-derived cell swelling and isotropy, but again this modulation was never complete.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the oryzalin treatment experiments with PME/PMEI induction.

claim: At the time of germination (0HPG), strong signal for de-methylated HG (LM19) was observed in basal and apical transverse sections.
source: At the time of germination (0HPG) we observed strong signal for de-methylated HG (LM19) in basal and apical transverse sections (Figure 6D,E) and weak signal for methylated HG (LM20; Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: At 0HPG, weak signal for methylated HG (LM20) was observed in basal and apical transverse sections.
source: At the time of germination (0HPG) we observed strong signal for de-methylated HG (LM19) in basal and apical transverse sections (Figure 6D,E) and weak signal for methylated HG (LM20; Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: At 24HPG, the de-methylated HG signal remained high in the slow-growing apical sections but was low in basal sections.
source: At 24HPG, the de-methylated HG signal remained high in the slow-growing apical sections but was low in basal sections (Figure 6F,G).
evidence: This is based on immunolocalization data shown in Figure 6F,G.

claim: At 24HPG, methylated HG exhibited lower signal in sections from slow growing apical regions and higher signal in sections from rapidly growing basal regions.
